sections.body: A measurement is a number and a unit, and the unit is not decoration. The same quantity can be written in many ways — 0.35 mm, 350 µm, 0.00035 m — and all three say exactly the same thing. Take the unit away and what is left is not a fact about the world; it is a fact about a piece of paper. This is why every serious drawing keeps the unit next to the number, and why an engineer who reads a bare number stops and asks what the number is a number of.
examples: The plate reads 12.5 mm, not 12.5.
Two suppliers quote 3.0 for the same part; only one of them says which 3.0.
A unit is part of the measurement, not a label stuck on it afterwards.
sections.heading: A number is not a measurement

terms.example: The unit is written after the number, with a space.
terms.gloss: A fixed quantity used as the standard for measuring something.

terms.example: Ten kilometres is a measurement; ten is not.
terms.gloss: A number together with the unit that gives the number its meaning.

sections.body: The International System of Units rests on seven base units. Every other unit in engineering is built out of them, and each base unit has a symbol that never changes, never takes a plural and never takes a full stop. A symbol is not an abbreviation: you write m for metre and you never write ms for metres, because ms means millisecond. Learn the seven symbols and you can read a line of specification without translating it.
examples: The symbol is m, not M and not mtr.
A symbol never takes a plural: 5 m, never 5 ms for metres.
The capital letters are not decoration either: A is the ampere and a is not.
sections.heading: The seven base units and the signs that stand for them

symbols.description: The letter m is the symbol of the metre, the base unit of length in the SI. Length is the quantity every other mechanical quantity is measured against, so it is the first unit an engineer learns. You meet it on a ruler, on the edge of a drawing, on the first line of a data sheet — whenever a distance is written: the height of a bolt, the width of a panel, the distance between two stars. Every engineer who measures anything at all reads it. It is written as a number, a space, then m: never a full stop, and never ms, because ms means millisecond.
symbols.label: m
symbols.meaning: metre — the base unit of length

symbols.description: The letters kg are the symbol of the kilogram, the base unit of mass in the SI. Mass is what stays the same wherever you take it; weight changes with gravity, mass does not. You meet it on a load rating, on a bill of materials, on the counter of a workshop — whenever something is weighed: a component, a payload, a person. The people who design the part and the people who load it are the ones who read it. It is written as a number, a space, then kg: the prefix kilo belongs to the unit, so the kilogram is written k and g together.
symbols.label: kg
symbols.meaning: kilogram — the base unit of mass

symbols.description: The letter s is the symbol of the second, the base unit of time in the SI. Time is the dimension that turns every other measurement into a rate. You meet it on a timing diagram, on the cycle time of a data sheet, on the second hand of a clock — whenever a duration is written: a cycle time, a dwell time, a reaction time. Anyone who measures how long something takes reads it. It is written as a number, a space, then s: watch out, 5 s is five seconds and 5 S would be wrong, but 5 ms is five milliseconds.
symbols.label: s
symbols.meaning: second — the base unit of time

symbols.description: The letter A is the symbol of the ampere, the base unit of electric current in the SI. Current is the flow of charge: how much charge passes a point of a circuit in one second, and every other electrical quantity is built on it. You meet it on the nameplate of a motor, on the rating of a fuse, on the first line of a power budget — whenever a current is written: the running current of a board, the start-up current of a pump, the current a sensor draws at rest. The people who size a cable and the people who size a supply are the ones who read it. It is written as a number, a space, then A: watch out, mA is a thousandth of an ampere and the ampere-hour (Ah) is a unit of charge, not of current.
symbols.label: A
symbols.meaning: ampere — the base unit of electric current

symbols.description: The letter K is the symbol of the kelvin, the base unit of thermodynamic temperature in the SI. Temperature is not the number a thermometer shows: a thermometer shows a point on an everyday scale, and the kelvin measures the energy of the particles themselves, so it never falls below zero. You meet it on the operating range of a part, on the control loop of a process, on the curve of a data sheet — whenever a temperature is written: a junction temperature, a storage temperature, the setpoint of a furnace. The people who design the part and the people who run the process are the ones who read it. It is written as a number, a space, then K: never a degree sign, because the degree sign belongs to the everyday scales, and watch out, the K of the kelvin is a capital K while the k of the kilo prefix is a small one.
symbols.label: K
symbols.meaning: kelvin — the base unit of temperature

symbols.description: The letters mol are the symbol of the mole, the base unit of amount of substance in the SI. A mole is a number of particles: the amount that holds as many particles as twelve grams of carbon-12, and it is the bridge between the mass of a thing and the number of things in it. You meet it on the certificate of a reagent, on the formula of a reaction, on the dosing sheet of a plant — whenever an amount is written: a concentration, a titration, the size of a batch. The chemist who mixes it and the engineer who scales it up are the ones who read it. It is written as a number, a space, then mol: never a full stop, and never a capital M, because M is the molar concentration and the two are not the same thing.
symbols.label: mol
symbols.meaning: mole — the base unit of amount of substance

symbols.description: The letters cd are the symbol of the candela, the base unit of luminous intensity in the SI: the light a source gives in one direction, judged by the eye of a person and not by an instrument alone. You meet it on the data sheet of an LED, on the specification of a luminaire, on the drawing of an optical bench — whenever a source of light is written: the backlight of a display, a signal lamp, a street light. The people who choose the lamp and the people who design the housing are the ones who read it. It is written as a number, a space, then cd: never a full stop, and watch out, cd/m² is a different thing — that is the luminance of a surface, and it is a derived unit.
symbols.label: cd
symbols.meaning: candela — the base unit of luminous intensity

sections.body: A prefix does not change what you are measuring; it changes how big the number is. Kilo means thousand, milli means thousandth. The prefix is written as a symbol in front of the unit with no space between them: 12.5 km, 3.2 mm. Every prefix is a power of ten, and every power of ten is a power of three as well: a kilometre is a thousand metres, and a thousand is ten times ten times ten. Mind the one trap in the whole system: milli and metre begin with the same letter, so 25 mA is twenty-five milliamperes while 25 m is twenty-five metres. The unit tells you which one you are looking at.
examples: A 3.5 mm screw needs a 3.5 mm hole, not a 3.5 m one.
The prefix changes the number, never the quantity: 5 km is 5000 m of road.
Gigabyte and gigahertz are different things; the prefix only says how big.
sections.heading: Prefixes: the words that multiply

rows: 5 nm — the wavelength of green light
12 μm — the width of a fine hair
3 cm — about the radius of a coin
5 kW — the power of a kettle
3 MHz — the clock speed of old electronics

sections.body: Dimensional analysis is a way to catch a formula before you trust it. You replace every quantity in the equation with the dimension it is measured in, add and subtract only things of the same dimension, and see whether both sides end up with the same dimension. A formula that balances is not proved, but a formula that does not balance is certainly wrong — and it usually fails for a reason you can name, such as an exponent that is off by one or a factor that was dropped when the formula was copied.
examples: Distance = speed × time: (m/s) × s = m. Both sides are lengths.
Energy = mass × speed²: kg × (m/s)² = kg·m²/s², which is the joule.
sections.heading: How to check a formula with dimensional analysis
steps: Write the formula with every quantity on one side and the result on the other.
Replace each quantity with its dimension: length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance, or luminous intensity.
Add and subtract only dimensions of the same kind; multiply and divide them as you would numbers.
Compare the two sides. The same dimension on both sides is necessary for the formula to be possible.
If the sides do not match, look for the quantity you measured wrongly or the factor you dropped.

sections.body: English puts the unit after the number, with a space: 12.5 mm, 3.2 kg, 20 °C. The space is not optional; it is what separates the number from the unit. A unit has no plural and no full stop: 5 m, never 5 m. or 5 ms. Degrees are written with a degree sign and no gap: 20 °C. When a number is a range, the word to or the dash carries it: 10 to 20 mm, or 10–20 mm. And a unit is lower case unless it carries the name of a person: 5 m, 5 kg, 5 mol, but 5 A for the ampere, 5 K for the kelvin and 5 °C for degrees Celsius.
examples: The tolerance is 10–20 mm, not ±20 mm, when the drawing means a range.
Write 5 m, not 5 m. — the full stop belongs to the sentence.
The unit is lower case unless it is named after a person: 5 A, not 5 a.
sections.heading: The grammar of a measurement

terms.gloss: The amount a measurement is allowed to differ from the nominal value.

terms.example: The nominal diameter is 12 mm with a tolerance of ±0.1 mm.
terms.gloss: The value a part is made to, before the tolerance is applied to it.

sections.body: Three words carry most of the technical meaning. A dimension is the kind of a quantity. A derived unit is a unit built out of the base units. Dimensional homogeneity is the property that makes an equation possible at all. Learn these three and a great deal of specification English stops being a list of phrases and starts being a set of rules you can apply yourself.
sections.heading: The words that go with the units

terms.example: Length and time are different dimensions, so you cannot add them.
terms.gloss: The kind of a quantity: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance or luminous intensity.

terms.example: The formula fails the test of dimensional homogeneity.
terms.gloss: The property of an equation whose two sides carry the same dimension.

terms.example: The newton is a derived unit of force.
terms.gloss: A unit made out of the base units, such as the newton or the joule.

sections.body: Most of the units you meet are not base units; they are built out of them. The newton is a derived unit of force: one kilogram moving one metre per second, once per second. The joule is a derived unit of energy, and the watt is a derived unit of power. Once you can name the base units inside a derived unit, a formula stops being a formula and starts being a sentence about the world.

equations.caption: One newton is one kilogram accelerating at one metre per second squared.
One joule is one newton moving a mass one metre.
Speed is distance divided by time.
Power is work divided by time.

examples: Force is measured in newtons, and a newton is a kilogram times a metre per second squared.
The power of an engine is not how hard it pushes; it is how fast it does work.
sections.heading: Derived units, and the units hiding inside them

sections.body: Converting is arithmetic; deciding which conversion is right is engineering. The number changes, the quantity never does. Convert 90 km/h into metres per second and the answer is 25 m/s — but the answer is only right if you also say that the number on the page now means something different from the number it meant before. A conversion table is a convenience; the formula behind it is the real tool, and the formula behind it is one line of arithmetic.
examples: 90 km/h is 25 m/s; the first number is a road speed, the second is a laboratory speed.
A conversion table is only a convenience: the formula behind it is the real tool.
sections.heading: Converting between units without losing the meaning

simulations.description: Move the slider to read the same speed in metres per second.
simulations.title: Speed in two scales

sections.body: A specification tells you the unit, the nominal value and the tolerance. It does not tell you the temperature the part was tested at, the material it was cut from, or the direction of the load. Units remove one kind of ambiguity, not all of them. When a drawing and a measurement disagree, do not reach for the conversion — check the conditions first.
sections.heading: What a specification does not tell you

sections.body: These are the sentences a drawing makes you say out loud. Learn them and reading a specification becomes a conversation rather than a puzzle.
examples: The bore is 25 mm H7, with a tolerance of +0.021 / 0.
The panel thickness is 1.5 mm, measured across the grain.
The torque is 4 N·m, applied with a calibrated wrench.
The material is rated for 200 °C continuous use.
Tolerance is not accuracy: the drawing says what is allowed, the measurement says what you got.
sections.heading: Sentences you can reuse when you read a drawing

item.summary: A number without a unit is not a measurement, and a formula whose two sides do not match in units is not a formula. After reading this you can name the seven base units, write a measurement the way a drawing expects it, check a formula with dimensional analysis, and explain why a converted number can be right in arithmetic and wrong in meaning.
item.title: Units, Dimensions and Dimensional Analysis
